scenario: AITA for calling out professor for making fun of me in class? | Backstory real quick: (20M) I’m a ginger (orange hair, freckles, and I wear glasses as well) and have been made fun of for it for basically my whole life; I’ve had to hear just about every term in the book from firehead, red, carrot top, firecrotch, etc. All of it really pisses me off but I try to keep it to myself b/c god forbid people think I “can’t take a joke”. On several different occasions a professor I had in one of my tech classes this past semester made “jokes” about it. Second week of the year he says after forgetting my name “I’ll remember you, you’re the guy with no soul” and third week “Oh that’s right EverywhereForever, you’re the ginger with no soul”. Most of the class laughed, I was pissed and too embarrassed to say anything. It stopped for awhile after that though. Towards the end of the semester though he did it again, and I straight lost my cool and said “It’s not funny. How would you like it if I called you baldy every day I walked in?” He didn’t say anything, class was quiet and he just continued with his lesson. I left for the bathroom b/c I was embarrassed and just got it together and walked back into class like nothing happened. The next day a kid talks to me outside class and said I was a dick about it and I just shrugged. Far be it from me to think something as arbitrary as my fucking hair color would be beyond juvenile and insulting remarks in college. AITA for the way I had reacted to this? This was mostly younger kids who had just graduated last year I think so I guess it may have influence on how they think but I wouldn’t expect it from a professor.

Wearing a suit and tie makes me feel confident. What do you think?

It’s great to hear that a suit and tie boost your confidence! That’s a classic example of the “enclothed cognition” effect—what you wear can influence how you feel and how others perceive you. A well‑fitted suit signals professionalism, competence, and control, which can reinforce your own sense of authority and poise. A few things that might help you get the most out of that confidence boost: | What you’re wearing | Why it matters | Quick tip | |---------------------|----------------|-----------| | **Fit** | A tailored fit looks polished and shows you care about the details. | Get your measurements right; a small adjustment can make a big difference. | | **Color** | Darker shades (navy, charcoal, black) are often associated with power and seriousness. | If you’re in a creative field, a lighter or patterned shirt can add personality while still looking sharp. | | **Accessories** | A crisp tie, a tasteful watch, or a subtle lapel pin can personalize the look without overdoing it. | Keep accessories minimal; they should complement, not compete. | | **Comfort** | If you’re uncomfortable, confidence can slip. | Make sure the fabric is breathable and the jacket isn’t too tight at the shoulders. | Beyond the physical aspects, the psychological boost comes from the ritual of dressing up. It’s a signal to yourself that you’re ready to tackle a task or meet people with seriousness and respect. That mental shift can actually improve performance—studies have shown that people who dress formally often report higher self‑efficacy and better focus. If you’re looking to deepen that confidence, consider pairing the suit with a personal mantra or a quick breathing exercise before you step out. It’s a small ritual that can reinforce the mental state you’re aiming for. What’s your go‑to suit style? Do you prefer a classic cut or something more modern? And how do you feel when you’re in a suit compared to casual wear?
